slides.title: From documents to chunks
lines: Source, parse, clean, chunk, add metadata, embed, index. Search returns chunks, not whole documents.

slides.title: Size and overlap
lines: Too big: one embedding averages many ideas, so the match is weak and tokens are wasted. Too small: the chunk loses its context. A common start: 200 to 500 tokens, 10 to 20% overlap. Tune with recall@k on your own questions.

slides.title: Respect structure
lines: Split on headings. Keep tables with their header row, code blocks whole, list items with their intro line. Trick: search small chunks, send the parent section to the LLM.

slides.title: Metadata
lines: Attach source, title, section, timestamp, version and permissions to each chunk. Metadata powers filters, citations, freshness and access control.

slides.title: Updates and deletes
lines: Track chunks by document ID. Hash chunks so only changed ones are re-embedded. Deleting a document must remove its chunks. Interview tip: always say how a deleted document disappears from the index.

questions.title: Big chunks
questions.prompt: Why do very large chunks hurt retrieval?
options: One embedding averages many topics, so the match is diluted
LLMs can't read more than 1,000 tokens
questions.keyIdea: One vector per chunk. The more ideas in a chunk, the blurrier its vector.
questions.why: Large chunks mix topics, so similarity to any one question drops, and they waste context tokens.

questions.title: Cut sentences
questions.prompt: You split every 300 tokens with no overlap, and a key sentence is cut in half. Best fix?
options: Add 10 to 20% overlap, or split on sentence boundaries
questions.keyIdea: Overlap and sentence-aware splits keep ideas whole.
questions.why: Neither half of a split sentence carries the full meaning. Overlap repeats the boundary text in both chunks.

questions.title: Split tables
questions.prompt: Spot the flaw: Markdown docs are cut every 500 tokens, splitting a pricing table in the middle.
options: Rows lose their header row, so answers about the table come out wrong
500 tokens is too small for Markdown
questions.keyIdea: Keep tables with their headers.
questions.why: A row like "Pro | 49 | 10" means nothing without "Plan | Price | Seats".

questions.title: Citation metadata
questions.prompt: Which metadata lets the answer show "Source: HR Handbook, updated Mar 2026"?
questions.keyIdea: Citations and freshness come from metadata, not from the vector.
questions.why: The vector is only for matching. Display info must be stored alongside it.

questions.title: Chunk count
questions.prompt: 2M documents, about 4,000 tokens each, 500-token chunks with 100-token overlap. About how many chunks?
questions.keyIdea: Chunks per doc is roughly doc tokens divided by (chunk size minus overlap).
questions.why: Each new chunk moves forward 400 tokens, so 4,000 / 400 = 10 chunks per doc, and 2M x 10 = 20M.

questions.title: Stale chunks
questions.prompt: Spot the flaw: when a document is edited, its new chunks are added but its old chunks stay in the index.
options: Outdated text still gets retrieved; replace a document's chunks by document ID
questions.keyIdea: Updates must replace, not just add.
questions.why: Old chunks still match questions and return stale or conflicting answers.

questions.title: Changed chunks
questions.prompt: 100K documents are edited per day, 10 chunks each, and about 2 chunks actually change per edit. With chunk hashes, how many chunks do you re-embed daily?
questions.keyIdea: Hash chunks and re-embed only what changed.
questions.why: 100K edits x 2 changed chunks = 200K.

ifWrong.0: That re-embeds every chunk of every edited document.

slides.title: What an embedding is
lines: A list of numbers that captures meaning. Similar meaning, nearby vectors. Documents and queries must use the same model.

slides.title: Bi-encoder retrieval
lines: Query and documents are encoded separately (two towers) and compared with a dot product or cosine similarity. Document vectors are computed ahead of time, which is why you can search millions in milliseconds.

slides.title: Dimensions and memory
lines: Raw size = vectors x dimensions x bytes per number (float32 = 4, float16 = 2, int8 = 1). More dimensions is not always better. Quantization saves memory for a small recall cost.

slides.title: Approximate search (ANN)
lines: Exact search compares every vector: too slow at scale. HNSW: a graph, fast with high recall, memory heavy. IVF: clusters, searches only a few (nprobe trades recall for speed). ScaNN: quantization plus re-scoring. Tune recall@k against p95 latency.

slides.title: Choosing and changing models
lines: Pick by evaluating on your own questions, not just a leaderboard: domain, languages, max input length, cost. A new model means re-embedding everything; run old and new indexes side by side and switch after evaluation.

questions.title: Fast search
questions.prompt: Why is bi-encoder retrieval fast enough for millions of documents?
options: Document vectors are computed ahead of time; a query is compared with a dot product
It reads the full text of every document per query
It runs the model on every document per query
questions.keyIdea: Precompute document vectors once; only the query is encoded at search time.
questions.why: Comparing vectors is cheap. Running a model on every document per query is not.

questions.title: Cosine score
questions.prompt: Two embeddings have cosine similarity 0.92. What does that mean?
options: The model sees them as very close in meaning
There's a 92% chance the answer is correct
questions.keyIdea: Cosine similarity measures direction of meaning, not word overlap or correctness.
questions.why: Two texts with different words can still score high if they mean the same thing.

questions.title: Float32 memory
questions.prompt: 10M chunks, 1,024 dimensions, float32. About how much raw vector memory?
questions.keyIdea: Size = vectors x dimensions x bytes per number.
questions.why: 10M x 1,024 x 4 bytes = about 41 GB.

ifWrong.0: That forgets the 4 bytes per float32 number.

questions.title: Int8 memory
questions.prompt: The same 10M x 1,024 vectors stored as int8 instead of float32. About how much memory?
questions.keyIdea: int8 uses 1 byte per number, a quarter of float32.
questions.why: 10M x 1,024 x 1 byte = about 10 GB.

questions.title: HNSW vs IVF
questions.prompt: Which statement about HNSW and IVF is true?
options: HNSW usually gives high recall at low latency but uses more memory
IVF compares the query with every vector
questions.keyIdea: Every ANN index trades recall, speed and memory.
questions.why: HNSW keeps a graph in memory. IVF searches only nearby clusters and is tuned with nprobe.

questions.title: Model mismatch
questions.prompt: Spot the flaw: queries now use a new embedding model, but document vectors were made with the old one.
options: Vectors from different models aren't comparable; re-embed the documents
It just runs a bit slower
Only the query cache needs clearing
The LLM will correct the mismatch
questions.keyIdea: Queries and documents must share one embedding model.
questions.why: Each model has its own vector space. Mixing them gives near-random results.

questions.title: IVF recall
questions.prompt: Your IVF index has low recall@10. Which knob helps most?
options: Increase nprobe to search more clusters (costs latency)
questions.keyIdea: nprobe is IVF's recall-versus-speed dial.
questions.why: Searching more clusters finds more true neighbors, at the cost of more comparisons.

slides.title: Dense vs sparse
lines: Dense (vectors) catches meaning and synonyms. Sparse (BM25 keyword search) catches exact terms: IDs, error codes, acronyms, rare names.

slides.title: Why hybrid wins
lines: Run both and merge. Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF): each list adds 1 / (k + rank), with k often 60. It merges by rank, so you never need to compare raw scores.

slides.title: Query rewriting
lines: Turn chatty follow-ups into standalone queries ("what about contractors?" becomes "PTO policy for contractors"). Fix typos, expand acronyms.

slides.title: Multi-query expansion
lines: Generate 3 to 5 versions of the question, search each, merge. Better recall, more latency and cost.

slides.title: Metadata filtering
lines: Restrict by product, date range, language or permissions. Filter inside the search, not after it, or you can lose all your top results.

questions.title: Error codes
questions.prompt: A user searches "ERR_4012 timeout" and dense-only search misses the right doc. Why?
options: Exact rare tokens like error codes aren't captured well by embeddings; add keyword search
The embedding dimension is too small
The chunk overlap is too large
questions.keyIdea: Keyword search catches exact strings that vectors blur.
questions.why: Embeddings capture meaning. "ERR_4012" has little meaning, but it is an exact match.

questions.title: Meaning match
questions.prompt: Which query is dense search better at than keyword search?
options: "how do I get my money back" finding a doc titled "Refund policy"
questions.keyIdea: Dense search matches meaning even with no shared words.
questions.why: "money back" and "refund" share no words but mean the same thing.

questions.title: RRF score
questions.prompt: With RRF and k = 60, a document is rank 1 in keyword search and rank 3 in dense search. Its fused score?
questions.keyIdea: RRF adds 1 / (k + rank) from each list.

questions.title: Follow-up queries
questions.prompt: Spot the flaw: in a chat, the user's follow-up is "what about contractors?" and retrieval searches just that text.
options: The query lacks context; rewrite it into a standalone query using the conversation
questions.keyIdea: Rewrite follow-ups into standalone queries before searching.
questions.why: "what about contractors?" alone matches almost anything.

questions.title: Multi-query cost
questions.prompt: What's the main trade-off of multi-query expansion?
options: Better recall, but more latency and cost
questions.keyIdea: More searches find more, but each one costs time and tokens.
questions.why: You add an LLM call to write the variants plus several searches to run and merge.

questions.title: Old pricing
questions.prompt: Spot the flaw: a user asks about 2026 pricing, and the 2023 pricing page ranks first.
options: No date or version filter; filter or boost by date and version metadata
The LLM temperature is too high
questions.keyIdea: Use metadata to keep results current.
questions.why: Old and new pricing pages look almost identical to an embedding.

questions.title: Multi-query latency
questions.prompt: Multi-query: an LLM rewrite takes 300 ms, then 4 searches of 40 ms each run in parallel, then merging takes 10 ms. How much latency does this add compared with one 40 ms search?
questions.keyIdea: Parallel searches cost the slowest one, not the sum.
questions.why: 300 + 40 + 10 = 350 ms total, versus 40 ms before, so about 310 ms more.

ifWrong.1: That runs the 4 searches one after another.
